Module 2 · H. S. Fogler, Elements of CRE 5e, §10.1 to §10.4.4

Adsorption, surface reaction, desorption and catalytic rate laws

How to postulate a mechanism, pick a rate-limiting step and turn it into a rate law written only in measurable partial pressures; then how to get the parameters from data and design a reactor with them.

HSF 10.2 to 10.4.4JMS 9-3 to 9-5 (same ideas)Class notes pp. 37–78Tutorial 2 Q1 · Tutorial 3

1Where we are heading

Rate laws in heterogeneous catalysis seldom follow power laws. Fogler teaches them "in reverse": first postulate mechanisms and derive the rate laws they imply, so that when you see data you recognise the form. In industry the order is the one in the figure.

Class notes, the same algorithm (p. 37)

2Steps 1 and 2 in brief (HSF 10.2.1, 10.2.2)

External diffusion (step 1)

Rate=kC (CAb−CAs),kC=DABδ\text{Rate} = k_C\,(C_{Ab} - C_{As}),\qquad k_C = \frac{D_{AB}}{\delta}Rate=kC​(CAb​−CAs​),kC​=δDAB​​

At low velocity the boundary layer δ\deltaδ is thick and transport is slow. As UUU rises or DpD_pDp​ falls, kCk_CkC​ rises until a plateau where CAb≈CAsC_{Ab}\approx C_{As}CAb​≈CAs​ and another step controls.

Internal diffusion (step 2)

Rate=kr CAs,kr∝1Dp (large pellets)\text{Rate} = k_r\,C_{As},\qquad k_r \propto \frac{1}{D_p}\ \text{(large pellets)}Rate=kr​CAs​,kr​∝Dp​1​ (large pellets)

In big pellets reactant is used up near the outside and the centre is wasted. Internal diffusion is not affected by the external flow. Small pellets: the surface steps control. Full treatment: Module 3.

4Surface reaction (HSF 10.2.4)

Once adsorbed, A can react in three kinds of ways. Each step is written as an elementary reaction, with surface concentrations for adsorbed species and partial pressures for gas-phase species.

Dual site A⋅S+S⇌B⋅S+SA\cdot S + S \rightleftharpoons B\cdot S + SA⋅S+S⇌B⋅S+SrS=kS(CA⋅SCv−CB⋅SCvKS)r_S = k_S\left(C_{A\cdot S}C_v - \dfrac{C_{B\cdot S}C_v}{K_S}\right)rS​=kS​(CA⋅S​Cv​−KS​CB⋅S​Cv​​) (10-16)dimensionless; kSk_SkS​ in g-cat/(mol⋅s)\mathrm{\text{g-cat}/(mol\cdot s)}g-cat/(mol⋅s)

5Desorption (HSF 10.2.5)

Desorption of C, C⋅S⇌C+SC\cdot S \rightleftharpoons C + SC⋅S⇌C+S, is simply adsorption of C read right to left:

10-20, 10-21rDC=kD(CC⋅S−PCCvKDC),KDC=1KC  ⇒  rDC=kD(CC⋅S−KCPCCv),rDC=−rADCr_{DC} = k_D\left(C_{C\cdot S} - \frac{P_C C_v}{K_{DC}}\right),\qquad K_{DC} = \frac{1}{K_C}\ \ \Rightarrow\ \ r_{DC} = k_D\left(C_{C\cdot S} - K_C P_C C_v\right),\qquad r_{DC} = -r_{ADC}rDC​=kD​(CC⋅S​−KDC​PC​Cv​​),KDC​=KC​1​  ⇒  rDC​=kD​(CC⋅S​−KC​PC​Cv​),rDC​=−rADC​

KDCK_{DC}KDC​ has units of atm; kDk_DkD​ of 1/s. The adsorption equilibrium constant of a species is the reciprocal of its desorption equilibrium constant.

6The rate-limiting step (HSF 10.2.6)

At steady state the three steps in series run at the same rate (there is no accumulation on the surface):

10-30−rA′=rAD=rS=rD-r'_A = r_{AD} = r_S = r_D−rA′​=rAD​=rS​=rD​

Usually one step is much slower. Think of an electric circuit: current III = rate, voltage EEE = driving force, resistances in series.

The Langmuir–Hinshelwood (Hougen–Watson) algorithm
  1. Postulate a mechanism: molecular or dissociative adsorption, single or dual site, Eley–Rideal. Write each step as reversible and elementary.
  2. Assume one step is rate-limiting. Its rate is the overall rate.
  3. For every other step, r/k≈0r/k \approx 0r/k≈0 (its rate constant is huge), so it is at quasi-equilibrium. Use these to express every Ci⋅SC_{i\cdot S}Ci⋅S​ in terms of partial pressures and CvC_vCv​.
  4. Write the site balance and solve for CvC_vCv​.
  5. Substitute into the rate of the limiting step. Lump constants into kkk. Replace ratios of constants by KPK_PKP​.
  6. Compare with data (initial-rate curves, runs with products added). If it disagrees, pick another limiting step; if all fail, another mechanism.
Why r/k≈0r/k\approx 0r/k≈0 for the fast steps

All three rates are equal. If kSk_SkS​ and kDk_DkD​ are very large, then rS/kSr_S/k_SrS​/kS​ and rD/kDr_D/k_DrD​/kD​ are tiny while rAD/kAr_{AD}/k_ArAD​/kA​ is not. Setting rS/kS=0r_S/k_S = 0rS​/kS​=0 gives the equilibrium relation of the surface step. (Strictly, one should compare kAPCk_AP_CkA​PC​ with kSk_SkS​ and kDk_DkD​ so that units match; the result is the same.)

Industrial adsorption-limited example

Ammonia synthesis on iron: H2+2S⇌2H⋅S\mathrm{H_2 + 2S \rightleftharpoons 2H\cdot S}H2​+2S⇌2H⋅S (rapid); N2+2S⇌2N⋅S\mathrm{N_2 + 2S \rightleftharpoons 2N\cdot S}N2​+2S⇌2N⋅S (rate-limiting: dissociative adsorption of N2\mathrm{N_2}N2​); successive hydrogenations N⋅S→NH⋅S→H2N⋅S→NH3⋅S\mathrm{N\cdot S \to NH\cdot S \to H_2N\cdot S \to NH_3\cdot S}N⋅S→NH⋅S→H2​N⋅S→NH3​⋅S and desorption of NH3\mathrm{NH_3}NH3​ (rapid).

Industrial surface-reaction-limited example

CO+NO→CO2+12N2\mathrm{CO + NO \rightarrow CO_2 + \tfrac12 N_2}CO+NO→CO2​+21​N2​ over copper: adsorption of CO and NO rapid; NO⋅S+CO⋅S⇌CO2+N⋅S+S\mathrm{NO\cdot S + CO\cdot S \rightleftharpoons CO_2 + N\cdot S + S}NO⋅S+CO⋅S⇌CO2​+N⋅S+S rate-limiting; N⋅S+N⋅S⇌N2⋅S+S\mathrm{N\cdot S + N\cdot S \rightleftharpoons N_2\cdot S + S}N⋅S+N⋅S⇌N2​⋅S+S and N2\mathrm{N_2}N2​ desorption rapid. CO2\mathrm{CO_2}CO2​ and N2\mathrm{N_2}N2​ are weakly adsorbed.

General form (class notes p. 59; Levenspiel eq. 18.1) rate=(kinetic term)×(driving force)(resistance term)n,e.g.−rA=k (pA−pB/K)1+KApA+KBpB\text{rate} = \frac{(\text{kinetic term})\times(\text{driving force})}{(\text{resistance term})^n},\qquad\text{e.g.}\quad -r_A = \frac{k\,(p_A - p_B/K)}{1 + K_Ap_A + K_Bp_B}rate=(resistance term)n(kinetic term)×(driving force)​,e.g.−rA​=1+KA​pA​+KB​pB​k(pA​−pB​/K)​

The resistance term (denominator) lists the adsorbed species; the power nnn is the number of sites in the limiting step.

Why KPK_PKP​ appears (10-38, 10-39)

At equilibrium rAD=0r_{AD}=0rAD​=0 gives PCe=PBePPe/(KSKC/KB)P_{Ce} = P_{Be}P_{Pe}/(K_SK_C/K_B)PCe​=PBe​PPe​/(KS​KC​/KB​). Thermodynamics says KP=PBePPe/PCeK_P = P_{Be}P_{Pe}/P_{Ce}KP​=PBe​PPe​/PCe​ for C⇌B+PC\rightleftharpoons B+PC⇌B+P. So KP=KCKS/KBK_P = K_CK_S/K_BKP​=KC​KS​/KB​, and it can be found from ΔG∘=−RTln⁡K\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln KΔG∘=−RTlnK. Every limiting case contains the same driving force PC−PBPP/KPP_C - P_BP_P/K_PPC​−PB​PP​/KP​, which vanishes at equilibrium, as it must.

Case II · Is the surface reaction rate-limiting? (kS≪kA,kDk_S \ll k_A, k_DkS​≪kA​,kD​)

Which one fits? (HSF 10.3.4)

Live: initial rate vs initial cumene pressure for each limiting step

Adsorption limiting: −rC0′=kPC0-r'_{C0} = kP_{C0}−rC0′​=kPC0​. Surface reaction limiting: −rC0′=kPC0/(1+KCPC0)-r'_{C0} = kP_{C0}/(1+K_CP_{C0})−rC0′​=kPC0​/(1+KC​PC0​). Desorption limiting: −rC0′=kDCt-r'_{C0} = k_DC_t−rC0′​=kD​Ct​. Shapes, not magnitudes, identify the step. The experimental curve for cumene (Fogler Fig. 10-18) rises and levels off, so the surface reaction is rate-limiting.

Adsorbing inerts (10-51 to 10-53)

An inert I that adsorbs, I+S⇌I⋅SI + S\rightleftharpoons I\cdot SI+S⇌I⋅S, with CI⋅S=KIPICvC_{I\cdot S} = K_IP_IC_vCI⋅S​=KI​PI​Cv​, just adds a term to the site balance: −rC′=k(PC−PBPP/KP)1+KCPC+KBPB+KIPI-r'_C = \dfrac{k(P_C - P_BP_P/K_P)}{1 + K_CP_C + K_BP_B + K_IP_I}−rC′​=1+KC​PC​+KB​PB​+KI​PI​k(PC​−PB​PP​/KP​)​. The rate falls as PIP_IPI​ rises, even though I does not react.

Class notes check

The notes (pp. 60–72) derive exactly these three cases, write the final form as −rC′=k(PC−PBPP/KP)1+KBPB+KCPC-r'_C = \dfrac{k(P_C - P_BP_P/K_P)}{1 + K_BP_B + K_CP_C}−rC′​=1+KB​PB​+KC​PC​k(PC​−PB​PP​/KP​)​, and label the numerator as the kinetic term times the driving force, and the denominator as the resistance term.

8Reforming catalysts and Table 10-4 (HSF 10.3.5)

Octane is raised by turning straight chains into compact molecules (n-pentane octane number 62, i-pentane 90). On bifunctional Pt/Al2O3\mathrm{Al_2O_3}Al2​O3​ (0.75 wt % Pt, Pt clusters about 10 Å on alumina pores 100–10 000 Å):

n-pentane ⇌−H2Pt n-pentene ⇌Al2O3 i-pentene ⇌+H2Pt i-pentane\text{n-pentane}\ \underset{\mathrm{Pt}}{\overset{-\mathrm{H_2}}{\rightleftharpoons}}\ \text{n-pentene}\ \underset{\mathrm{Al_2O_3}}{\rightleftharpoons}\ \text{i-pentene}\ \underset{\mathrm{Pt}}{\overset{+\mathrm{H_2}}{\rightleftharpoons}}\ \text{i-pentane}n-pentane Pt⇌−H2​​​ n-pentene Al2​O3​⇌​ i-pentene Pt⇌+H2​​​ i-pentane

Focus on the isomerisation N⇌IN \rightleftharpoons IN⇌I on alumina. Table 10-4 applies the algorithm.

Try 1: dual-site mechanism

N+S⇌N⋅SN + S\rightleftharpoons N\cdot SN+S⇌N⋅S; N⋅S+S⇌I⋅S+SN\cdot S + S \rightleftharpoons I\cdot S + SN⋅S+S⇌I⋅S+S; I⋅S⇌I+SI\cdot S \rightleftharpoons I + SI⋅S⇌I+S.

−rN′=rS=kS(CvCN⋅S−CI⋅SCvKS)-r'_N = r_S = k_S\left(C_vC_{N\cdot S} - \frac{C_{I\cdot S}C_v}{K_S}\right)−rN′​=rS​=kS​(Cv​CN⋅S​−KS​CI⋅S​Cv​​) CN⋅S=KNPNCv,CI⋅S=KIPICv,Cv=Ct1+KNPN+KIPIC_{N\cdot S} = K_NP_NC_v,\quad C_{I\cdot S} = K_IP_IC_v,\quad C_v = \frac{C_t}{1 + K_NP_N + K_IP_I}CN⋅S​=KN​PN​Cv​,CI⋅S​=KI​PI​Cv​,Cv​=1+KN​PN​+KI​PI​Ct​​ −rN′=k (PN−PI/KP)(1+KNPN+KIPI)2,k=kSCt2KN, KP=KNKSKI-r'_N = \frac{k\,(P_N - P_I/K_P)}{(1 + K_NP_N + K_IP_I)^2},\quad k = k_SC_t^2K_N,\ K_P = \frac{K_NK_S}{K_I}−rN′​=(1+KN​PN​+KI​PI​)2k(PN​−PI​/KP​)​,k=kS​Ct2​KN​, KP​=KI​KN​KS​​

Try 2: single-site mechanism (the one that fits)

N+S⇌N⋅SN + S\rightleftharpoons N\cdot SN+S⇌N⋅S; N⋅S⇌I⋅SN\cdot S \rightleftharpoons I\cdot SN⋅S⇌I⋅S; I⋅S⇌I+SI\cdot S \rightleftharpoons I + SI⋅S⇌I+S.

−rN′=rS=kS(CN⋅S−CI⋅SKS)-r'_N = r_S = k_S\left(C_{N\cdot S} - \frac{C_{I\cdot S}}{K_S}\right)−rN′​=rS​=kS​(CN⋅S​−KS​CI⋅S​​) =kSKN(PN−PIKP)Cv= k_SK_N\left(P_N - \frac{P_I}{K_P}\right)C_v=kS​KN​(PN​−KP​PI​​)Cv​ −rN′=k (PN−PI/KP)1+KNPN+KIPI,k=kSCtKN-r'_N = \frac{k\,(P_N - P_I/K_P)}{1 + K_NP_N + K_IP_I},\quad k = k_SC_tK_N−rN′​=1+KN​PN​+KI​PI​k(PN​−PI​/KP​)​,k=kS​Ct​KN​

These are Tutorial 3 Q2 (i) and (ii). Step 2 of the algorithm says start with the surface reaction: more than 75 % of heterogeneous reactions that are not diffusion-limited are surface-reaction-limited. If two models fit, discriminate statistically (residuals). A fit never proves a mechanism; spectroscopy is needed for that, but a misfit does disprove one.

10PSSH and temperature dependence (HSF 10.3.6, 10.3.7)

Pseudo-steady-state hypothesis

Instead of setting r/k≈0r/k\approx 0r/k≈0 for the fast steps, treat each adsorbed species as a reactive intermediate whose net rate of formation is zero:

ri⋅S∗=0r^*_{i\cdot S} = 0ri⋅S∗​=0

Used mainly when more than one step is rate-limiting. (Class notes p. 74: PSSH gives CT⋅S≈CB⋅SC_{T\cdot S}\approx C_{B\cdot S}CT⋅S​≈CB⋅S​ roughly constant, rT⋅S≈rB⋅S≈0r_{T\cdot S}\approx r_{B\cdot S}\approx 0rT⋅S​≈rB⋅S​≈0.)

High temperature

kkk follows Arrhenius and rises with TTT. Adsorption is exothermic, so every KiK_iKi​ falls with TTT: coverage drops and the denominator tends to 1.

−rA′=kPA1+KAPA+KBPB → high T  −rA′≈kPA-r'_A = \frac{kP_A}{1 + K_AP_A + K_BP_B}\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{high }T\ }\ -r'_A \approx kP_A−rA′​=1+KA​PA​+KB​PB​kPA​​  high T ​ −rA′​≈kPA​

or −rA′≈k(PA−PB/KP)-r'_A \approx k(P_A - P_B/K_P)−rA′​≈k(PA​−PB​/KP​) if reversible. This is why Levenspiel (Module 3) is happy with first-order kinetics.

10.4.1 Deducing the rate law from the data

  1. Reversibility. Runs 3 (PM=0P_M=0PM​=0) and 5 (PM=1P_M=1PM​=1) give 41.6 and 42.0: the reverse reaction does not matter. Treat as irreversible.
  2. Methane. Runs 1 and 2: quadrupling PMP_MPM​ leaves the rate unchanged, 71.0→71.371.0 \to 71.371.0→71.3. Methane is not adsorbed (or KMPM≪1K_MP_M\ll 1KM​PM​≪1); it goes straight to the gas, like propylene for cumene.
  3. Benzene. Runs 3, 4, 6 (and 7 with PB=0P_B=0PB​=0): rate falls 71.8→41.6→19.7→17.171.8 \to 41.6 \to 19.7 \to 17.171.8→41.6→19.7→17.1 as PBP_BPB​ goes 0→1→4→50 \to 1 \to 4 \to 50→1→4→5 atm. Benzene is in the denominator: it adsorbs. −rT′∼1/(1+KBPB+… )-r'_T\sim 1/(1 + K_BP_B + \dots)−rT′​∼1/(1+KB​PB​+…). "If it is in the denominator, it is probably on the surface."
  4. Toluene. Runs 10–15: rate rises with PTP_TPT​ at low pressure (47→71.347 \to 71.347→71.3) and levels off at high pressure (131→133131 \to 133131→133). −rT′∼PT/(1+KTPT+… )-r'_T \sim P_T/(1 + K_TP_T + \dots)−rT′​∼PT​/(1+KT​PT​+…).

What Fogler wants you to notice
  • Pressure drop costs conversion: 68.2 % instead of 79 %. For this feed, eliminating or minimising pressure drop would raise benzene production by up to 61 million pounds a year. Neglecting ΔP\Delta PΔP "could have been very embarrassing".
  • PBP_BPB​ passes through a maximum (Fig. E10-2.2). PB=yBPP_B = y_BPPB​=yB​P. Near the middle to the end of the bed benzene is barely forming, so yBy_ByB​ stops rising, but the total pressure keeps falling, so PBP_BPB​ falls too.
  • Conversion rises quickly and then slows: the partial pressures fall with both conversion and pressure, and the benzene produced occupies sites.

Fogler's closing analysis

Both the packed bed and the fluidised CSTR need a lot of catalyst for this small feed. To reduce the catalyst weight, raise the temperature, provided side reactions and catalyst decay do not become a problem.

13Self-test

Derive the rate law for A⇌BA \rightleftharpoons BA⇌B (single site) if adsorption of A is rate-limiting and B is adsorbed.

rAD=kA(PACv−CA⋅S/KA)r_{AD} = k_A(P_AC_v - C_{A\cdot S}/K_A)rAD​=kA​(PA​Cv​−CA⋅S​/KA​). Surface reaction equilibrium: CA⋅S=CB⋅S/KSC_{A\cdot S} = C_{B\cdot S}/K_SCA⋅S​=CB⋅S​/KS​. Desorption equilibrium: CB⋅S=KBPBCvC_{B\cdot S} = K_BP_BC_vCB⋅S​=KB​PB​Cv​. So CA⋅S=KBPBCv/KSC_{A\cdot S} = K_BP_BC_v/K_SCA⋅S​=KB​PB​Cv​/KS​ and

rAD=kACv(PA−KBPBKSKA)=kACv(PA−PBKP),KP=KSKAKBr_{AD} = k_AC_v\left(P_A - \frac{K_BP_B}{K_SK_A}\right) = k_AC_v\left(P_A - \frac{P_B}{K_P}\right),\quad K_P = \frac{K_SK_A}{K_B}rAD​=kA​Cv​(PA​−KS​KA​KB​PB​​)=kA​Cv​(PA​−KP​PB​​),KP​=KB​KS​KA​​ Ct=Cv(1+KBPBKS+KBPB) ⇒ −rA′=kACt(PA−PB/KP)1+(KB/KS+KB)PBC_t = C_v\left(1 + \frac{K_BP_B}{K_S} + K_BP_B\right)\ \Rightarrow\ -r'_A = \frac{k_AC_t(P_A - P_B/K_P)}{1 + (K_B/K_S + K_B)P_B}Ct​=Cv​(1+KS​KB​PB​​+KB​PB​) ⇒ −rA′​=1+(KB​/KS​+KB​)PB​kA​Ct​(PA​−PB​/KP​)​

Note A is absent from the denominator: when adsorption of A is limiting, A⋅S\mathrm{A\cdot S}A⋅S is not in equilibrium with gas A.

A rate law is −rA′=kPA(1+KAPA+KBPB)2-r'_A = \dfrac{kP_A}{(1 + \sqrt{K_AP_A} + K_BP_B)^2}−rA′​=(1+KA​PA​​+KB​PB​)2kPA​​. What does each feature say?

KAPA\sqrt{K_AP_A}KA​PA​​: A adsorbs dissociatively. Squared denominator: the limiting step involves two sites (e.g. the two A fragments reacting on adjacent sites). KBPBK_BP_BKB​PB​: product B adsorbs molecularly and inhibits.

Why does the initial rate become independent of cumene pressure at high pressure if the surface reaction limits?

At high PC0P_{C0}PC0​, KCPC0≫1K_CP_{C0}\gg1KC​PC0​≫1 and almost every site is covered by cumene (CC⋅S→CtC_{C\cdot S}\to C_tCC⋅S​→Ct​). The rate kSCC⋅Sk_SC_{C\cdot S}kS​CC⋅S​ cannot grow any more: −rC0′→k/KC=kSCt-r'_{C0}\to k/K_C = k_SC_t−rC0′​→k/KC​=kS​Ct​.

In the toluene data, how do you know hydrogen is not adsorbed but toluene is?

Rate doubles each time PH2P_{H_2}PH2​​ doubles (runs 7–9): first order at all pressures, so no saturation, so negligible coverage. Toluene shows saturation (runs 12–15 nearly flat), the signature of adsorption in the denominator.

What is PSSH and when would you use it instead of the rate-limiting-step method?

The net rate of formation of each adsorbed intermediate is set to zero, ri⋅S∗=0r^*_{i\cdot S}=0ri⋅S∗​=0. Use it when no single step is much slower than the others (two or more comparable steps).

At high temperature, why do catalytic rate laws often reduce to power laws?

Adsorption is exothermic, so adsorption constants fall with TTT. Coverages become small, ∑KiPi≪1\sum K_iP_i\ll1∑Ki​Pi​≪1, the denominator tends to 1, and −rA′≈kPA-r'_A\approx kP_A−rA′​≈kPA​.

Show that for any limiting step in cumene decomposition the rate vanishes at equilibrium.

Each form contains PC−PBPP/KPP_C - P_BP_P/K_PPC​−PB​PP​/KP​ with KP=KCKS/KB=(PBPP/PC)eqK_P = K_CK_S/K_B = (P_BP_P/P_C)_{eq}KP​=KC​KS​/KB​=(PB​PP​/PC​)eq​, which is zero at equilibrium. It comes from combining the quasi-equilibrium relations of the fast steps with the driving force of the slow step.

Fogler P10-5: −rE′=kPEPH1+KEPE-r'_E = \dfrac{kP_EP_H}{1 + K_EP_E}−rE′​=1+KE​PE​kPE​PH​​ for ethylene hydrogenation. Suggest a mechanism.

E+S⇌E⋅SE + S \rightleftharpoons E\cdot SE+S⇌E⋅S (equilibrium); E⋅S+H2(g)→A⋅SE\cdot S + H_2(g) \rightarrow A\cdot SE⋅S+H2​(g)→A⋅S (Eley–Rideal, limiting); A⋅S⇌A+SA\cdot S \rightleftharpoons A + SA⋅S⇌A+S with ethane weakly adsorbed. Then −rE′=kSCE⋅SPH-r'_E = k_SC_{E\cdot S}P_H−rE′​=kS​CE⋅S​PH​, CE⋅S=KEPECt/(1+KEPE)C_{E\cdot S} = K_EP_EC_t/(1+K_EP_E)CE⋅S​=KE​PE​Ct​/(1+KE​PE​), which gives the rate law with k=kSKECtk = k_SK_EC_tk=kS​KE​Ct​. Hydrogen reacting from the gas explains why it is in the numerator but not the denominator.

In Fogler Example 10-2, why does the benzene partial pressure pass through a maximum along the packed bed, and what does the pressure drop cost?

PB=yBPP_B = y_BPPB​=yB​P. Early in the bed benzene forms quickly, so yBy_ByB​ rises faster than PPP falls. Towards the end almost no benzene forms, yBy_ByB​ levels off, and the falling total pressure pulls PBP_BPB​ down. Pressure drop lowers the conversion of the 10 000 kg bed from 0.79 to 0.682, and the bed cannot exceed 10 197 kg or the exit pressure would fall below 1 atm.
